SMTO-EXE-0133 — A web browser step took too long

GUID: b799b73d-0135-594f-986c-391759e7df6c
Slug: browser-timeout
Domain: EXE · Subsystem: browser

What happened

  • SMTO waited for a step on the web page, such as a click or typing, but it didn't finish in time. Part of it may still have happened on the page.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Ask SMTO in the conversation to look at the current page and tell you what it shows. A slow page may have accepted the click or typing even though SMTO stopped waiting for it.
  2. If the step clearly didn't happen, ask SMTO to wait for the button or text to appear first, and to allow up to a minute. SMTO normally waits about 10 seconds per step, which can be too short for a slow website.
  3. Open the same website yourself and check that it loads and responds normally. If the site is slow or down for you too, the delay is coming from the website, not from SMTO.

What success looks like

  • The page shows the result you expected, and SMTO reports the step as finished.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them, with the website address, to the person who manages SMTO. Don't ask SMTO to repeat a form submission or payment until you've checked on the website that it didn't go through.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • A non-navigation browser operation exceeded its timeout_ms deadline (default 10 s, maximum 60 s) or raised a TimeoutError; effect_unknown reports whether the action had already started.

What this means

  • A non-navigation browser action reached its deadline or raised the recognized TimeoutError class, with attempted effects retained separately. The retained effect boundary and original session identity govern recovery. Browser page content remains untrusted, diagnostic rendering adds no navigation or model call, and mutations are not automatically replayed.

Why this can happen

  • A non-navigation browser action reached its deadline or raised the recognized TimeoutError class, with attempted effects retained separately.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect operation type, page state and effect_unknown before deciding whether a bounded observation or other action is justified.

How to fix it

  • Check effect_unknown in the receipt and read the page with browser.page_info or browser.snapshot before repeating anything. For slow pages use browser.wait_for with a locator or text, or a larger timeout_ms (up to 60000); BrowserService never retries clicks, input or submissions itself.
  • Inspect the page and effect_unknown flag. Use a bounded wait if appropriate; reconcile before repeating a mutation.

Retry and execution caution

  • Inspect the page and effect_unknown flag. Use a bounded wait if appropriate; reconcile before repeating a mutation.

How to verify the fix

  • The original action is reconciled; a timeout does not itself trigger another click, input or submission.

What not to do

  • Do not replay uncertain mutations, scan CDP endpoints, or export cookies/passwords/storage.

Technical notes

  • The retained effect boundary and original session identity govern recovery. Browser page content remains untrusted, diagnostic rendering adds no navigation or model call, and mutations are not automatically replayed.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
